intro:
Middle Eastern restaurant takeout gets busy fast, especially at lunch, dinner, and on weekends. An AI phone host can answer those calls, take the order, and send it to the kitchen without making your team stop what they are doing.

For a shawarma shop, falafel counter, or family-run Mediterranean spot, the main win is simple: fewer missed calls, cleaner orders, and less time spent repeating the same menu questions. ROAL is built for that kind of phone work, and it can read your live menu, hours, and address from your public pages or an uploaded menu.

sections.h2: What should an AI phone host do for Middle Eastern takeout?
sections.body:
For a Middle Eastern restaurant, the phone is usually full of the same questions: “Do you have chicken shawarma?” “What comes with the platter?” “Is pita included?” “What time is pickup?” An AI phone host should handle those basics clearly and send real orders to the kitchen.

ROAL does that from the restaurant’s live menu. It takes items, sizes, modifiers, and notes; collects the caller’s name and phone; quotes a ready time; and confirms the order back. It also answers common questions about hours, address, parking, and the menu. If a caller asks about catering, a complaint, a serious allergy concern, or wants a manager, it hands that to staff with a summary.

A practical phone flow for a takeout spot looks like this:
1. Greet the caller.
2. Ask whether they want pickup or delivery.
3. Take the order item by item.
4. Repeat the total and ready time.
5. Confirm the name and number.
6. Send the ticket to the kitchen screen.

Example line: “Thanks for calling. I can take your takeout order now, or answer menu and hours questions.”

sections.h2: How do you set it up without a big project?
sections.body:
Setup should be quick, because owners do not have time for a long tech job. With ROAL, the owner pastes the restaurant website, Google Maps link, or just “Name, City” at /try. ROAL reads the menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages, then builds a phone host in about a minute.

If the menu is in a PDF or even menu photos, the owner can upload it too. Then they test-call the host right in the browser. No sign-up is needed for that test step. The owner also picks the host’s voice and name, so it sounds like a fit for the restaurant.

A simple setup checklist:
- Have your website or Google Maps listing ready.
- Make sure your menu and hours are current.
- Test items that matter most, like platters, wraps, salads, sides, and family meals.
- Check whether sold-out items are marked correctly.
- Try a real order from your browser before going live.

If you want the broader setup flow, see [How it works](/how-it-works) or the [ROAL facts](/facts).

sections.h2: How does call forwarding work for a busy takeout line?
sections.body:
Once the owner claims the host, ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically. The restaurant keeps its own number, and the owner forwards that number to ROAL. They can forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered. Forwarding can be turned off any time.

This matters for Middle Eastern takeout because a lot of calls come in during short windows. If your cashier is already packing orders, a forwarded call can still get answered. If a caller asks something the host cannot answer, it lands in the inbox and the owner answers once; the host learns it from then on.

Phone forwarding codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a call. Common examples include:

| Situation | Common code examples |
| --- | --- |
| Forward all calls | *72 on many landlines and some carriers; **21*number# on some GSM carriers |
| Turn forwarding off | *73 or ##21# |
| Forward unanswered calls | **61*number# |
| Forward busy calls | **67*number# or *71 on some Verizon plans |

For business VoIP systems, forwarding is often set in the web portal. If you want a quick reference, use [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

sections.h2: What should you say for menu items, add-ons, and sold-out dishes?
sections.body:
Middle Eastern menus often have a lot of choices in a small space: chicken, beef, lamb, falafel, hummus, baba ghanoush, rice, salad, extra sauce, spicy sauce, pita, and combo platters. The phone host should handle those choices without forcing the caller to repeat themselves.

ROAL reads from the live menu, so it does not offer items marked sold out. That helps avoid awkward calls when the kitchen is out of a popular item. It can also handle modifiers and notes, like extra garlic sauce, no onion, or “light rice.”

Here is a simple script pattern your staff can expect:
- “I have your chicken shawarma platter with rice, salad, and extra garlic sauce.”
- “Would you like it mild or spicy?”
- “I’ve got your pickup ready in about 20 minutes.”

Example menu setup tips:
1. Make your best-sellers easy to find.
2. Use clear names for platters, wraps, and family trays.
3. Keep side options and add-ons consistent.
4. Mark sold-out items right away.
5. Write out common notes the kitchen understands.

If you also run a mix of dine-in and takeout, a [menu, hours and allergen questions](/use-cases/menu-questions) page can help you think through the most common caller questions.

sections.h2: How much can takeout calls cost compared with other options?
sections.body:
For many owners, the question is not whether calls matter. It is what the phone problem is costing each month. Delivery apps commonly charge restaurants roughly 15-30% commission per order. Many AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599, whether or not orders come in. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call.

ROAL uses a different model: $0.90 per completed phone order, meaning a confirmed order whose ticket reached the kitchen screen. There is no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free. Billed monthly.

Here is a simple example you can swap for your own numbers:
- Say your average takeout order is $28.
- A 20% delivery app commission would be about $5.60 per order.
- ROAL would be $0.90 for a completed order.
- On 100 completed orders, that is $90 with ROAL.
- Plug in your own average ticket and monthly order count to compare.

If you want to compare your own numbers, try the [AI phone host cost calculator](/tools/phone-host-cost-calculator) or the [phone orders vs delivery apps](/compare/delivery-apps) page.

sections.h2: How do you handle tricky calls without slowing the line?
sections.body:
Not every call should be handled by a phone host. That is especially true in a Middle Eastern restaurant, where callers may ask about a big catering tray, a missing order, a severe allergy, or a manager issue. ROAL is built to pass those calls to staff with a summary.

It also takes reservation requests when needed, but it does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however the restaurant already takes it. That keeps the process aligned with how many takeout places already work.

A good staff handoff plan is simple:
- Catering request: kitchen or manager gets the summary.
- Complaint: staff sees the caller’s name, number, and issue.
- Allergy-sensitive question: staff reviews it directly.
- Manager request: the call is escalated.

Example staff note: “Caller wants a 12-person platter for Saturday at 6 p.m. Asked about trays, rice, salad, and sauce portions.”

If you are short-staffed, this matters even more. The goal is not to replace your team. It is to keep the phone from pulling your best person away from food, packing, and pickups. You can read more on [short-staffed shifts](/use-cases/short-staffed) or [catering inquiries](/use-cases/catering).

sections.h2: What is a practical rollout plan for one location or several?
sections.body:
Start with one location, even if you plan to expand later. For a single Middle Eastern takeout shop, begin with the busiest hours first. Let the phone host answer during lunch rush, dinner rush, or when staff is tied up. Once the flow feels right, extend it to all calls if you want.

For multi-location owners, each location can have its own host and its own menu details. That helps if one branch has different prices, different hours, or a few different specials. ROAL also includes multi-location menus in the dashboard, plus call history, transcripts, recordings, a menu editor, hours, FAQs, and upsell suggestions.

A rollout checklist:
1. Pick the first location.
2. Clean up hours, address, and menu items.
3. Test the top 10 takeout orders.
4. Forward calls during one service window.
5. Review the inbox for unanswered questions.
6. Update the menu or FAQ once, then use it going forward.

ROAL was built by Venkata Vamsi, a founder in Jersey City, NJ, and it is live for US restaurants. If you want to try a hosted version for your own menu, [build a free test host](/try).
